title: Where August's river comes from
teaches: Groundwater in the spaces between grains, Darcy's law, baseflow, and gaining and losing streams
summary: **Groundwater fills the spaces between grains.** Under western Washington it is almost never an underground lake or river: it sits in the pores of sand and gravel and in cracks in rock.
**The water table is where the pores fill up.** Above it the ground holds air and some water; below it every pore is full, and a well fills to its level.

**Darcy's law: flow follows the drop in head.** Double the drop across a layer and the flow doubles; double the thickness and it halves; and each material has its own conductivity, from free-flowing gravel to almost sealed clay.
**Groundwater is slow.** In sand it creeps a fraction of a metre a day, so water reaching a river may have fallen as rain years before.
**Baseflow is the river the ground supplies.** A gaining stream is fed through its bed and banks wherever the water table stands above it, and in a dry August that seep is nearly all the river.

**Snow decides when the ground is refilled.** In 2015 a normal amount of precipitation fell as rain, ran off in winter, and left the aquifers draining from February, so rivers reached record lows by August.
**A losing stream leaks into the ground.** Where the water table lies below the bed, the river shrinks as it flows.
**A well near a creek captures its baseflow.** Once the well takes more than the ground was feeding that stretch, the creek turns from gaining to losing, and that happens sooner as summer goes on.

**On islands fresh water floats on salt.** For every metre the water table stands above sea level, fresh water reaches about 40 metres below, so overpumping near the shore draws salt water up into wells.

parts.title: A normal winter, a dry river

blocks.text: The winter of 2014 to 2015 did not look like the start of a drought. Rain gauges in western Washington collected close to their usual totals between November and March, and the rivers ran high through the winter storms. What was missing was the cold. Storm after storm came in warm, so precipitation that normally falls as snow in the Cascades and the Olympics fell as rain and ran straight off. On 1 April, the date snow surveyors use to take the measure of the year's store, the mountain snowpack was a small fraction of normal, and in parts of the Olympics there was almost none.

In May the governor declared a drought across the whole state. By August many rivers in western Washington were running at or near the lowest flows ever measured for the time of year, and some small lowland creeks had shrunk to pools. Newspapers called it a snow drought: a drought in a year with plenty of rain.

Lesson 1 described the snowpack as a reservoir that holds winter's water until summer. That accounts for the rivers in May, June and July of a normal year. It does not account for August and September, when the snow below the high peaks has long since melted and weeks go by with hardly any rain, and yet the rivers keep running. Snoqualmie Falls, which roars in February, thins to a fraction of itself by late summer, but it never stops. Something keeps feeding it. This lesson follows that water underground, and then comes back to 2015.

**The underground lake.** Ask someone to draw groundwater and you will often get a cave: a dark lake under the hills, or a stream running through a tunnel in the rock. Such places exist, in limestone country where water has dissolved channels through the rock, but they are rare, and there are almost none under western Washington. Nearly all groundwater is somewhere less dramatic: in the spaces between grains of sand and gravel, and in the cracks of solid rock.

Fill a jar with gravel and pour water in. A jar that looks full of stone takes a surprising amount, about a third of its volume. That share of empty space is the material's **porosity**. Clean sand and gravel have porosities of about 25 to 40 percent. Underground, below a certain depth, all that space is already full of water: a hillside of saturated gravel is roughly a third water, held in countless small connected rooms.

Dig down from the surface and the pores change. Near the top they hold some air and some water clinging to the grains, like a sponge that has been wrung out. Lower down every pore is full. The surface where the full zone begins is the [[water table|ground]]: dig a hole below it and water seeps in from the sides until it stands at that level, and no higher. A layer of sediment or rock that holds water and lets it move freely enough to supply a well is an **aquifer**.

blocks.caption: Groundwater lives in the pores. Above the water table the pores hold air and water; below it they are full, and a well fills to that level. Clay holds the most water of the three, but its pores are so small that the water barely moves.

blocks.text: Under the Puget lowland the best aquifers were laid down by ice. When the Vashon glacier pushed south about 17,000 years ago (the Geology course tells that story), its meltwater spread broad sheets of clean sand and gravel, called **outwash**, in front of it. The ice then rode over the outwash and plastered it with a dense, compacted mix of clay, sand and stones, glacial **till**: the hardpan that a Seattle gardener's spade bounces off. Many of the region's wells go down through the till to reach the outwash beneath it.

Henry Darcy was the chief engineer of Dijon, in Burgundy, a town that had long been short of clean water. In the 1830s and 1840s he gave it a covered aqueduct about 12 kilometres long from a spring in the hills, and pipes under the streets to public fountains, one of the best water supplies in Europe for its day. In 1856 he described the whole system in a long book, *Les Fontaines publiques de la ville de Dijon*. The part that made his name is in an appendix.

The town wanted to filter its water through beds of sand, and Darcy needed to know how big a filter would have to be. In 1855, with the engineer Charles Ritter, he set up an upright iron pipe about 2.5 metres tall and 35 centimetres across, put a layer of sand in it, and ran water down through the sand. Gauges filled with mercury measured the water's pressure above and below the sand. He changed how thick the sand was and how hard the water was pushed, and timed how much came out at the bottom.

The push is best measured as **head**: the height to which water would rise in a tube open to the air, at that point.[^head] Water underground moves from high head to low. The figure is Darcy's column, with gauges showing the head above and below a metre of sand. Before you change it, guess what one change does.

blocks.caption: Darcy's column: water runs down through a metre of sand, pushed by the drop in head between the gauge above the sand and the gauge below it. The plot shows the flow out of the bottom. Choose the grain and set the drop.
blocks.task: Guess, then find the drop that doubles the flow

blocks.text: Darcy's result was that simple. The flow is proportional to the drop in head across the sand, and inversely proportional to the sand's thickness: double the drop and the flow doubles, double the thickness and it halves. A wider pipe passes more, in proportion to its area. And each sand has its own number for how easily water passes through it, now called its **hydraulic conductivity**. This is **Darcy's law**, and every groundwater calculation since rests on it.[^law]

Try the grains. Water passes through clean gravel about ten million times more easily than through clay. Clay is porous, often more so than sand, but its pores are so small that the water clings to the flakes and barely moves.[^clay] That is why a layer of clay or till can hold up the water in the sand above it, or seal in an aquifer below.

**How fast is groundwater?** The water table usually slopes gently, a metre or so of drop in every hundred metres. Put that slope into Darcy's law for a sandy aquifer and the water creeps along at around half a metre a day, about two football pitches in a year. Rain that soaks in two kilometres from a river can take a decade to reach it. The river carries the same water two kilometres in under an hour.

parts.title: The water table meets the river

blocks.text: The water table is not flat. It rises under hills, where rain soaks in, and falls toward valleys, following the shape of the land in a smoothed-out way. Groundwater moves down its slope, from high head to low, as Darcy's law says it must. In a valley the lowest head is the river. Wherever the water table stands above the river's surface, groundwater seeps into the channel through its bed and banks, along every metre of its length. A river fed this way is a **gaining stream**, and the water it gains is [[baseflow|ground]].

Lesson 2's hydrograph showed a river rising quickly after a storm and then falling back along a long, slowly flattening tail. The quick part is the storm's own rain running off the land. The tail is baseflow: the aquifers along the valley draining into the river, more and more slowly as their water tables sink. After weeks without rain it is all that is left. In a dry August nearly all the water in a lowland river has come out of the ground, and much of it fell as rain months or years before.

That is also why creeks feel so cold in August. A few metres down, the ground hardly notices the seasons and stays near the year's average air temperature, about 10 °C (50 °F) in the Puget lowland. Groundwater seeps out at that temperature, so in summer it is the coldest water in the river, and fish gather where it comes in.

Now back to 2015. In a normal year the snow melts from April into July. Some of the melt runs straight into the rivers, and much of it soaks into the soil and gravel of the mountain valleys, topping up their aquifers just before the dry season begins. In 2015 the same water arrived as rain in December and February, when the ground was already full, so most of it ran off at once, raising winter floods instead of summer stores. With no snowmelt to refill them in spring, the aquifers started draining months earlier than usual. By August their water tables, and the rivers they feed, had fallen to record lows.

Not every river gains. Where the water table lies below the riverbed, water leaks out of the channel into the ground, and the river shrinks as it flows. That is a **losing stream**. Many rivers in dry country lose water for much of their length, and some sink into their own gravel in summer. In western Washington most rivers gain, but a reach can switch. A creek crossing a fan of coarse gravel at a mountain front may lose water there and gain it back lower down, and in a long dry spell a small creek can go from gaining to losing as the water table beside it falls.

People can switch it too. A well beside a creek pumps from the same aquifer that feeds the creek, and lowers the water table around itself in a cone. At first the well draws on water stored in the ground nearby. As pumping goes on the cone spreads until it reaches the creek, and from then on every litre the well lifts is a litre that would have reached the creek as baseflow, or that the creek now loses back into the ground. Hydrologists call this **capture**. The figure is a valley in cross-section: a creek at the foot of a rock wall, an aquifer rising away from it, and a well.

blocks.caption: A creek, its aquifer and a well, in cross-section. Set the weeks since the last real rain and how hard the well pumps; the arrow at the bank shows which way water crosses it. A model, with the pumping run long enough to settle.
blocks.task: Guess, then make the creek lose water to the ground

blocks.text: The creek turns from gaining to losing once the well takes more than the ground was feeding that stretch of creek. That threshold falls as summer goes on, because baseflow falls with the water table. Play the weeks with the well at 15 litres a second: harmless in June, it turns the creek around by September. Washington's courts and legislature have been arguing over exactly this since 2016.[^hirst]

**On a bluff.** After a wet spell, walk the beach under one of the high bluffs on the Sound, at Discovery Park, Carkeek Park or along the Whidbey shore, and look partway up the face for a line of dark wet ground, moss, ferns or trickles. That line is often where water soaking down through sand meets a layer of clay it cannot pass and runs out sideways: a water table perched on clay, seen in cross-section. Seep lines like these are where many of Seattle's landslides begin.

On an island the aquifer has salt water on every side. Rain soaking into Whidbey, Camano or the San Juan Islands forms a lens of fresh water that floats on the seawater filling the ground below sea level, the way oil floats on vinegar. Because fresh water is only about 2.5 percent lighter than seawater, the lens floats deep: for every metre the water table stands above sea level, the fresh water reaches about 40 metres below it.[^lens] The same rule works in reverse. Pump a well near the shore hard enough to lower the water table by a metre, and the salt water beneath rises by about 40 metres toward it. Wells along island shores are watched for this, **seawater intrusion**, because once a well turns salty it can stay that way for years.

East of the mountains, Spokane drinks from the opposite extreme. Its aquifer lies in boulders and gravel dumped by the Ice Age floods that the Geology course follows across eastern Washington, and water moves through it metres a day, far faster than through Puget lowland sand. Even there it is water moving through the spaces between stones; the stones are large, and so are the spaces.

blocks.caption: Six questions on groundwater and baseflow
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Which picture of groundwater under western Washington is closest to the truth?
choices: Water filling the spaces between grains of sand and gravel, and the cracks in rock
Lakes and streams flowing through caves and tunnels in the bedrock
A sheet of open water lying on a bed of clay, with the soil floating above it
items.why: Nearly all groundwater sits in pores and cracks. Underground lakes and rivers need rock that dissolves, such as limestone, and are rare here.

items.ask: Darcy doubled the drop in head across his column of sand and kept everything else the same. What happened to the flow?
choices: It hardly changed, because the sand set the rate
It went up four times, since pressure and speed both rose
items.why: Darcy's law: the flow through a porous layer is proportional to the drop in head across it, and inversely proportional to the layer's thickness.

items.ask: A lowland river is still running after six weeks without rain in August. Where is most of its water coming from?
choices: Groundwater seeping into the channel from the aquifers along the valley
Snow still melting on the low and middle slopes of the mountains
Rain from the last storm still draining off the surface of the hillsides
items.why: That is baseflow. Surface runoff is gone within days of a storm, and by August the snow below the high peaks has melted; the ground drains for months.

items.ask: In the winter of 2014 to 2015 western Washington had near-normal precipitation, yet many rivers ran at record lows the next August. Which explanation is best?
choices: It fell as rain instead of snow, ran off in winter, and left no spring melt to refill the aquifers before summer
Most of the winter rain evaporated in the warm air before it could reach the ground
Heavy pumping for irrigation drained the rivers because the summer was hot
items.why: The amount was ordinary; the timing was not. Without snowmelt in spring, the aquifers that feed summer baseflow began draining months early.

items.ask: A well beside a creek pumps steadily for months. When does that stretch of creek start losing water to the ground?
choices: When the well takes more than the ground was feeding that stretch of creek
As soon as the pump is switched on, whatever its rate
Never, because a well draws on deep water that creeks cannot reach
items.why: Once the well's cone of lowered water table reaches the creek, its water comes from the creek's baseflow. Take more than that and the creek must supply the rest.

items.ask: Why can heavy pumping near the shore of an island turn a well salty?
choices: Fresh water floats on seawater in the ground, and each metre the water table falls lets the salt water rise about 40 metres
Seawater soaks down from the beach through the soil at every high tide
Pumping draws salt out of the rock grains into the water around the well
items.why: Fresh water is about 2.5 percent lighter than seawater, so the fresh lens floats about 40 times as deep below sea level as the water table stands above it.

head.title: Head
head.text: Head adds up two things: how high the water is, and how hard it is pressed. Water deep in an aquifer under a hill can be at higher head than water at the surface of a valley below, so groundwater can flow sideways or even upward, into the bed of a river. It always flows from high head to low.

law.title: Darcy's law in symbols
law.text: Q = K × A × Δh ÷ L: the flow Q equals the conductivity K times the area A times the drop in head Δh, divided by the thickness L. A typical K is about 1 centimetre a second for clean gravel, about a thousandth of that for fine sand, and a billionth or less for clay. Darcy's law holds while the water creeps; in very coarse gravel with a steep drop the flow turns eddying and the law begins to fail.

clay.title: Why clay holds water and keeps it
clay.text: Clay particles are flakes thousandths of a millimetre across, and the gaps between them are smaller still. Water in such narrow gaps is held by its attraction to the flakes' surfaces, so a clay can be half water by volume and still pass almost none of it.

hirst.title: The Hirst decision
hirst.text: In 2016, in Whatcom County v. Hirst, the Washington Supreme Court ruled that a county could not approve a new house supplied by a household well without first checking that the well would not take water from streams whose flows the state protects. Building in rural areas stalled until the legislature passed the Streamflow Restoration Act in 2018, which allows such wells with fees and watershed plans to offset what they capture.

lens.title: Forty to one
lens.text: This is the Ghyben-Herzberg rule, found by Willem Badon Ghyben in the Netherlands in the 1880s and Alexander Herzberg in Germany in 1901. Seawater is about 1.025 times as dense as fresh water, so a column of fresh water balances a column of seawater 1/40 shorter: each metre of fresh water above sea level holds the boundary about 40 metres down. Real lenses mix at their base, so the rule is an estimate.
